The water surrounding Boston is dotted with sailboats year-round, and now that summer’s nearly begun, you’re sure to see plenty of them cruising through the Charles River and Boston Harbor on pleasant, breezy days.

The question is: How can you get on one?

As a matter of fact, you don’t need to know a sailor or own a sailboat to go sailing in Boston. (You will have to take a few classes, though.) Once you’ve gotten started, it’s a skill you can hone over time and enjoy for summers to come, according to local sailing instructors.

"We have people who in one season go from complete beginners to sailing in high wind conditions, sailing on more advanced boats,” said Anna Braun, education and volunteer manager at the Boston nonprofit Community Boating Incorporated. “So, if you're really dedicated to it and you come a decent amount, I would say you can become a good sailor in a season.”

Think this might be the season you set sail? First, check out the tips below from Braun, Boston Sailing Center general manager David Bryan and Community Boating member and volunteer Thea Berthoff so you don’t get stuck “in irons” as you get started.

How hard is sailing, really?

Operating a sailboat isn’t like renting a kayak. The watersport has enough jargon to warrant its own glossary, and you’ll need to complete a training course before you can take the helm. But all in all, “it’s not that hard,” Bryan said. “It just takes a lot of patience and understanding that there’s a lot of variables.”

The biggest variable, of course, is the wind. A sailboat needs wind pressure to move, but the gusts can be tricky to harness.

“If the wind always blew from the same direction, you could learn how to sail in an afternoon,” Bryan said. “But the wind's always changing direction, increasing or decreasing in velocity, so it can be a little frustrating when you're a beginner.”

It takes practice to learn how to detect where the wind's coming from, he added. But once you finally do, “then you can learn how to trim your sails and get to where you're headed.” (See? Sailing really does have its own lingo — but more on that in a moment.)

First, let’s talk about lessons. A monthly membership at a sailing school can run you anywhere from $99 to over $1,000. So before you get on a boat, you’ll want to ask yourself: do you want to do this for a summer, or for your life? How you answer will help you choose a local program that fits your goals.

Community Boating, which launches out onto the Charles River, has a basic, 30-day trial membership that comes with introductory sailing lessons and an opportunity to take the boat out on your own for $99. You’ll have to take two courses — rigging and shore school — totaling four hours of instruction. You’ve also got the option to go on a guided sail with an instructor after that. Once the first month is through, the membership renews at $175 a month, which grants you unlimited boat sign outs and free beginner and intermediate classes so you can keep learning.

Boston Sailing Center, which launches onto the harbor out of Lewis Wharf, also offers an introductory sailing program that comes with a monthlong student membership for a one-time fee of $1,200. Their program totals 22 hours of instruction, which you can either take over a weekend, over four weeks or over a singular vacation week. Bryan says the center’s courses are well suited for complete beginners or people who might have sailed as kids and need a refresher.

“And when you complete the course … you have access to the boats you learned on for 30 days afterwards, which is a great way to kind of practice and internalize what you just learned,” Bryan said. Once that trial is through, however, you’ll need to sign up for a daysailing membership, which can range from $765 (for a monthly membership) to $1,930 (for a yearly membership). But that’s still a lot cheaper than buying and maintaining your own boat.

At a glance, you can tell Community Boating and Boston Sailing Center offer programs with two different levels of time commitment. There are even more sailing schools in Boston, like Courageous Sailing, First Reef Sailing and the Piers Park Sailing Center that offer a range of memberships and lessons for you to choose from.

Not interested in joining a boating club? If you or a friend already have sailing experience, you can also rent a four-person sailboat for two hours for $99 from Community Boating from now through Oct. 31. (But before you can head out, the skipper will need to answer some questions from the dockmaster on duty, so make sure to brush up on your sailing knowledge.)

The learning curve

As you’re learning, both Bryan and Braun agreed sailing regularly is key to picking up the sport quickly and safely.

“It's good to get out at least once a week on your own,” Bryan said. Like any skill, getting better at sailing “depends on how much time you want to put in,” Braun added.

Learning the basics of handling your boat includes knowing how to “trim your sails” — that is, adjust your sails to the wind — as you venture out on the water. Here are a few important terms to get you started on that:

Bryan reiterated that navigation errors like sailing into the wind and sailing into shallow water are common when first learning to sail.

But “the most common mistake is when people get into a kind of a tight situation, sometimes trying to force the boat into that area that it doesn't really sail,” Bryan said.

Braun, who has taught more than 200 people to sail during her time at Community Boating, said she thinks the biggest thing people struggle with is confidence. “ People get super intimidated by seeing people run into the bridge or capsize,” she said.

But the instructors noted such errors are inevitable when you’re first starting out.

“We're dealing with mishaps pretty much every day with every beginner. No matter what, whenever you start, you're gonna flip your boat, you're gonna run into the bridge, you're gonna hit the island,” Braun added. “But everything always works out, and people's reaction afterwards is always, ‘that wasn't so bad.’”

Field Guide to Boston: Discover — and rediscover — your Boston.

And you’re not alone out on the water. Both Boston Sailing Center and Community Boating have safety teams you can contact via VHF radio for help during any sail — though it’ll cost you $115 per man hour for a rescue at Boston Sailing Center.

New hobbies, new friends

Berthoff, a member of Community Boating, began sailing four years ago. “I kept walking by and biking by on the Charles River Esplanade, and seeing how beautiful and fun it looked out there, and I was like, ‘What better thing to do in the Boston area?’” she told me.

“ The culture has been incredibly supportive, especially whenever you have a question or you're wondering about something, or you wanna just practice out on the river a little bit,” Berthoff said. “There is somebody who's gonna be in your corner, who's gonna be willing to help you out and to just give you an extra push.”

Boston Sailing Center also boasts a tight-knit community. Bryan says many of the students in the introductory program will pair up for sailing practice; eventually becoming members of the club.

“We do see a lot of the same folks coming back year after year,” Bryan said. “Some of our best members are those who have purchased a boat, realize how expensive it is, and then come back and join our program so they don't have to do the maintenance.”

Where to set sail

Once you’ve built up your confidence at the helm, Braun, Bryan and Berthoff suggest trying these routes as you traverse through Boston Harbor or the Charles:

“There are so many beautiful spots on the river,” said Braun. “There’s the MIT Boathouse; there are different public docks on the Esplanade. So bouncing back and forth between them and just seeing what else is going [on] around Boston is my favorite.”

Berthoff prefers sailing bridge to bridge on the Charles.

“I love going from the Longfellow all the way to the Mass Ave. Bridge, especially because it encourages me to practice,” she said. “Being able to be fast or slow, to take in everything that's on the water and enjoy all of the different views that are along the way.”

Launching out of Boston Harbor for a quick sail, Bryan said the first island you’ll hit is Spectacle Island and a round trip takes less than three hours.

“If you have some time, one of my favorite routes is to go out around the Graves Lighthouse, and then continue out in Broad Sound there, and go around Boston Light and come back in past Hull. You're rounding more islands and it's just a beautiful sail,” he said.

P.S. — It’s not just locals setting sail this summer. The Tall Ships will be returning to Boston for the first time in nearly a decade this July. Click here to learn more about those gigantic multi-sail ships and their role in MA250 celebrations.
